analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The drilling bill drew 49 cosponsors but never received a committee vote and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the 1980 law banning oil and gas production in the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and direct the Interior Secretary to hold lease sales there within a year of enactment. It would offer at least 200,000 acres per sale by sealed competitive bid, grant pipeline rights-of-way across the plain, and declare — by act of Congress — that drilling is compatible with the refuge's purposes. Its sponsor was the Alaska congressman who chaired the committee the bill was sent to, and 49 members signed on in support; the committee still never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, which would win long-term leases to explore and drill on up to roughly 1.5 million acres of a national wildlife refuge, plus pipeline operators and the Alaska state and local governments that would collect royalty and tax revenue and see jobs tied to North Slope development.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the prohibition in the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act against producing oil and gas from the Arctic Refuge and any leasing leading to it, opening the roughly 1,549,000-acre coastal plain to leasing [S2][S3].

Directs the Interior Secretary to hold the first lease sale within 12 months of enactment, offering at least 200,000 acres, with leases going to the highest qualified sealed bid at a royalty of no less than 12.5 percent [S3].
Grants rights-of-way and easements across the coastal plain for oil and gas transportation, overriding the normal access rules in the 1980 Alaska lands act [S3].
Supporters argued the drilling would reduce dependence on foreign oil, add domestic supply, create jobs, and raise federal revenue through royalties and taxes [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The American public, which owns the refuge. The bill permanently opens a designated wildlife area to industrial development, with the risk borne by the caribou herds, birds, and subsistence communities that depend on the coastal plain, while the fair-market-value royalties and environmental protections in the bill rest on the Interior Secretary's discretion and are hard to enforce in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public that owns the refuge

drawbacks.text: The bill declares by congressional flat that coastal plain drilling is compatible with the refuge's purposes and states that no further findings or decisions are required to implement that determination, preempting the environmental review process the 1980 law contemplated [S3].

It caps the land the Interior Secretary may close to drilling at 45,000 acres of 'Special Areas' and names the act as the Secretary's sole authority to close any coastal plain land, sharply limiting future protections [S3].
It restricts court challenges: lawsuits over actions under the act must be filed within 90 days, and challenges to drilling regulations can be heard only by the D.C. federal appeals court [S3].
By its own findings, a new North Slope field takes 10 or more years to develop, so the bill would not produce near-term relief at the gas pump even if enacted [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's direct financial gains would flow mainly to the companies that win the leases; the public would receive royalties at fair market value and possibly some future domestic supply, but would give up permanent protection of a unique wildlife area and would have little practical ability to challenge the drilling program in court. The energy-security benefit, by the bill's own timeline, would arrive a decade or more after drilling began.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee, chaired by its own sponsor, but the committee never took it up, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young (R-AK) introduced the bill on June 16, 1999, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Resources [S5].
49 members cosponsored it — 47 Republicans, 1 Democrat, and 1 Independent [S4].

The only further actions were an introductory speech by the sponsor on June 17 and a June 29 referral to the Interior Department for comments; the Resources Committee never held a markup or vote on the bill [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 106th Congress on January 3, 2001, having never reached the House floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never got a vote, the coastal plain stayed closed to drilling: oil companies gained no leases, and the public kept the refuge intact through the end of the century. Efforts to open the area continued in later Congresses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept the refuge unleased

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-AK) and Chairman, House Committee on Resources
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as committee chair, controlled the committee to which it was referred; the committee still never voted on it.

against.name: House Committee on Resources
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the June 1999 referral; no markup, no vote, no report on the bill.

against.name: Environmental and conservation organizations
against.role: National preservation groups opposing Arctic Refuge drilling
against.what_they_did: Campaigned through the late 1990s and 2000s to keep the coastal plain closed to drilling, framing the issue as protection of caribou, birds, and subsistence communities.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: His administration opposed opening the Arctic Refuge to drilling throughout his term, making enactment impossible during the 106th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: of 49 cosponsors, 47 were Republicans, with just 1 Democrat and 1 Independent.

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and production
industries.note: The bill repeals the statutory drilling ban and directs Interior to sell leases on the refuge's coastal plain within a year, handing companies long-term access to a publicly owned resource; the public would collect a 12.5%-minimum royalty but bear the permanent environmental risk to a national wildlife refuge.

The bill directs the Secretary to grant rights-of-way and easements across the coastal plain for oil and gas transport, bypassing the standard access process in the 1980 Alaska lands act; more North Slope barrels would feed existing pipeline and tanker capacity.

industries.industry: Alaska state and North Slope local governments
industries.note: The bill's findings cite support from the State of Alaska, the North Slope Borough, and Inupiat communities, which would share in revenue and receive employment and contracting provisions for Alaska Natives; their gain comes from development the bill would otherwise prohibit.
